nudge: Hi there. The park is empty at 7. Just saying.
No pressure. But your shoes looked at the door again.
Small run, small-talk-free. Twenty minutes?
Headphones optional. People optional. Run recommended.
The route you like is still there. It kept the spot.
A run is a meeting with one attendee. Attendance is great.
Nobody will ask how you are out there. That is the whole point.
Today could use a loop. Any loop. Even a small one.
You don’t have to talk to anyone to lace up.
Out, back, shower, quiet. A good afternoon, honestly.
The pavement has no opinions about your pace.
A run counts even if nobody knows about it. Especially then.
Quick one? The world will still be loud when you get back.
Legs: available. Weather: fine. Excuses: respectfully declined.
Thirty minutes where your phone only counts kilometres.
Running is the one hobby where leaving early is called finishing.
Your energy might say no. Your energy has been wrong before.
One run. Zero conversations. Infinite smugness. Reasonable deal.
The quiet streets are quietest right now. Take the hint.
The best part of a run is the bit where nobody can reach you.
A gentle reminder that you own a pair of running shoes.
Not a push. A nudge. The difference is about five minutes.
There is a version of today where you ran. It is slightly better.
If you need a reason: there isn’t one. That’s allowed.
A run is a long walk that’s in a hurry to be alone.
Your route misses you. Routes don’t say that often.
Twenty minutes outside beats twenty minutes of thinking about it.
It’s a good day to be a dot moving across a map.
The only group run that works: you, and your shadow at a distance.
Reminder: fresh air is free and asks no questions.
rest: Yesterday’s run is still counting. Rest is part of the plan.
You ran. Today the job is sitting down and being pleased about it.
Rest day. Your legs are quietly rebuilding. Let them.
Nothing to do today. That was the point of yesterday.
Recovery is also running. Just the invisible kind.
Good run yesterday. Today, be mildly insufferable about it, privately.
The muscles are at work. You are not required to supervise.
A day off keeps the running from becoming a chore. Enjoy the sofa.
You earned a slow day. Collect it.
Post-run report: energy up, world still too loud. Both normal.
Nothing to prove today. Already done.
Your legs would like a word: thank you, and please, not today.
Rest well. The road is patient and so is this app.
Running yesterday was the hard part. Resting today is the smart part.
Two days in a row is allowed. So is one. You pick.
quiet: It’s been a few days. The route didn’t go anywhere.
Quiet week? A short run is a good way to end it.
No run in a bit. No problem. One easy loop resets everything.
A few days off is normal. A few more is also normal. Either way, hello.
The shoes are getting suspicious. Reassure them.
If the week got loud, a run is the quietest room you own.
Gentle reminder: a bad short run is better than a great planned one.
Haven’t run this week? The week isn’t over, and nobody’s keeping score. Except, quietly, you.
A run would fix roughly one thing today. That’s a decent ratio.
Your pace from last week is unbothered. It’ll wait.
Restarting is just starting with better shoes.
The hardest kilometre is the one between the door and the pavement.
gap: A week off happens. The road didn’t go anywhere.
Hi again. No lecture. Just a door, and a route past it.
Life got in the way. Life does that. A short run gets it back out.
Welcome back, whenever that is. There’s no form to fill in.
A long gap just means the first run back will feel like a discovery.
Nothing is lost. Fitness is loyal; it leaves slowly and comes back quickly.
No streak to rescue. Just a run to enjoy, if you fancy it.
Start small. The map doesn’t care how small.
Someone has to run around that lake. It might as well be the quiet one.
You don’t owe anyone a comeback. You can just go for a run.
If today is the day: lovely. If not: tomorrow is also a day.
The first run back is mostly about proving the shoes still fit.
weather: It’s raining. Nobody will be out. You know what that means.
Cold out. Fewer people. Almost like the weather is on your side.
Grey skies clear the paths. Best time to have them to yourself.
Dark early. Headlamp on. The world shrinks to one quiet circle.
Drizzle is the introvert’s crowd control.
Wind in your face means the route is doing half the thinking.
Bad weather, empty park. Honestly, perfect.
Puddles don’t make conversation. Ideal running companions.
A run in the rain is a shower you take on the way to the shower.
The fog is in. Even the joggers who wave can’t see you.
morning: Good morning. One short note, then I’ll leave you be.
The streets are still asleep. Join them, moving.
Early run: the day hasn’t started asking things of you yet.
Morning. The park has roughly three people and a heron.
Sunrise runs: you’re out before anyone can suggest a group one.
Coffee, shoes, door. Conversation not required.
The quiet hour is open. Reservation for one.
Morning light and an empty towpath. Hard to improve on.
evening: Evening. The day is done talking. Go somewhere it can’t follow.
A short run before dark. Then the sofa can have you.
Dusk run: everyone else is indoors being social. Enjoy the outdoors being not.
The last light is the best light. Also the emptiest.
A loop before dinner. Nobody at the table needs to know.
End the day as a dot on a map. Quiet, moving, yours.
Evening air, low sun, no crowd. Take the easy win.
Tomorrow can be loud. Tonight, a run and then nothing.

rhythm: {day}, around now. You usually go about this time. Just mentioning it.
Your hour is coming up. The route is where you left it.
{day} is apparently a running day for you. The park agrees.
This is roughly when you go. No pressure, just the hour.
The usual {day} slot is nearly here. The shoes have noticed.
In about an hour it’s your time. Nobody else has booked it.
Your {day} run, if you want it. It’s been reliable company.
Habit check: {day}, late enough to wake up, early enough to matter.
window: Rain until {time}, then dry. The paths stay empty a bit longer than the clouds do.
Wet now. Dry from {time}. Most people won’t notice. You will.
Dry from {time}. The puddles will have cleared the park for you.
It eases off around {time}. Fewer people, fresher air, same route.
last: That’s the last nudge for a while. The app will be here, quietly, whenever.
Going quiet now. If you want the reminders back, just go for a run.
Last one from me for a bit. No hard feelings. No feelings at all, technically.
reflectLines: Energy now, before the shower wins. One tap.
How do you feel, compared to before? Tap to note it.
afterRunLines: Nobody saw that. Which was the plan.
Energy check: probably up. Science, roughly.
That’s a run. No feed, no kudos, no notes. Just yours.
Shower, tea, silence. In that order.
The map has a new line on it. Only you can see it.
Good. Now go be unavailable for a while.
Legs did the talking. Everything else can stay quiet.
A run finished is a conversation you didn’t have to have.

topics.title: Aches, pains, and when to stop

tips.text: Run-walk is not cheating. It is how a great many people finish their first 5K, and plenty of marathons too.
The first ten minutes feel worst for almost everyone while the body switches on. Judge the run after that, not before.
Start slower than feels necessary. Going out too fast is the classic beginner mistake, and nobody hands out medals for minute three.
You can turn around whenever you like. A run that ends early is still a run, and arguably a well-managed one.
You are a runner from the first one. There is no minimum distance and no membership card.
Rest days are when you actually get fitter. The run is the request, recovery is the delivery.
For the first few weeks, add time before speed. Same easy pace, a few more minutes.
Some runs feel heavy for no reason. That is normal and tells you very little. The next one usually feels fine.
A wet cotton shirt can rub your nipples raw after about 5 km. Wear a synthetic or merino top, and add tape or balm for longer runs.
tips.source: Jogger’s nipple: Levit, NEJM 1977; Mailler & Adams, Br J Sports Med 2004

tips.text: “Jogger’s nipple” has been a medical term since 1977. A plaster costs less than the dignity.
tips.source: Levit, N Engl J Med 1977

tips.text: Thighs that touch will raise the matter around km 4. Anti-chafe balm or short tights end the discussion.
Chafe starts at seams, labels, waistbands and the edge of a sports bra. Balm goes on before the run. After is just called regret.
Dried sweat leaves salt on the skin, which works like very fine sandpaper. On hot or long runs, rinse off soon after.
If something stings in the shower, that is where you chafed. Make a note. That spot gets balm next time.
Rain makes chafing worse, because wet fabric drags. Snugger clothes and a little balm help more than a heavier jacket.
Pick running shoes by how they feel in the shop, not by colour or a gait scan. Comfort is the best guide researchers have found.
tips.source: Nigg et al., Br J Sports Med 2015

tips.text: Being told you “overpronate” is not a reason to panic. In a study of 927 new runners in neutral shoes, pronators were not injured more.
tips.source: Nielsen et al., Br J Sports Med 2014

tips.text: Leave about a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Feet swell and slide forward downhill.
Try shoes on in the afternoon, with your running socks. Feet are a little bigger later in the day, as they are on a run.
For many people the longest toe is the second one. Size for that toe, not the big one.
Runners who alternated between more than one pair had a 39% lower injury risk in one study of 264 runners. A second pair is also a dry pair.
tips.source: Malisoux et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports 2015

tips.text: New shoes get a few short runs first. Not the long run. Never the race.
That extra eyelet at the top of the shoe has a job. A heel-lock lace there stops your heel slipping and saves toenails.
A black toenail usually means shoes a touch too small or downhills taken too fast. Try half a size up.
Shoes have no expiry date. Around 500 to 800 km, or when they start to feel flat, is a common time to swap. The evidence is thin, your legs are a better judge.
Expensive is not safer. Spend on fit. Carbon-plated race shoes make fast runners faster, and easy Tuesday loops mostly more expensive.
Wet shoes: pull out the insoles, stuff them with newspaper, keep them away from the radiator. Heat melts the glue.
Dress as if it were 5 to 10 °C warmer. You will be cold for five minutes and right for the rest. Warm at the door means overdressed.
Cotton socks hold water and make blisters. Synthetic or merino running socks are the cheapest upgrade in running.
Nothing new on race day. Not shoes, not shorts, not the breakfast someone online swears by.
A well-fitted sports bra matters more than any shirt. Unsupported breasts move several centimetres with every stride, and that is felt.
tips.source: Research Group in Breast Health, University of Portsmouth

tips.text: Shorts with a zip pocket mean no bag, no belt and no faff. Keys, card, done.
A cap keeps rain off your glasses and sun off your face. The most useful running gear nobody photographs.
Gloves before a hat. Fingers go cold first and come back last.
Reflective bits on your ankles and wrists are seen sooner than on your chest, because drivers recognise moving limbs as a person.
tips.source: Biomotion studies: Wood, Tyrrell et al.

tips.text: Two thin layers beat one thick one. You can take one off and tie it round your waist like it is 1994.
Most runs should be easy enough to talk in full sentences. You will not be talking to anyone. But you could.
tips.source: Talk test: Persinger et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2004

tips.text: Your easy pace can be a minute or more per km slower than your fastest 5K pace. That is not lazy, that is how it is done.
Uphill: shorter steps, same effort, let the pace drop. The hill does not know your average.
There is no magic 180 steps a minute. But if you overstride, steps about 5 to 10% quicker and shorter take load off the knees and hips.
tips.source: Heiderscheit et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011

tips.text: Windy day: run out into the wind and home with it behind you. Tired you will be grateful.
There is no correct breathing pattern. Mouth, nose, both. If you cannot finish a sentence, you are no longer running easy.
GPS pace wobbles under trees and between tall buildings. Your effort does not. Trust the one in your chest.
Finishing a little faster than you started is called a negative split. It feels smug in the best way.
For runs under an hour, most people need nothing on the go. A drink before and after, and thirst is a fine guide.
tips.source: ACSM fluid replacement position stand, 2007

tips.text: Drinking far beyond thirst on long runs can dilute your blood’s sodium, which is dangerous. Drink to thirst, not to a schedule.
tips.source: Hyponatraemia consensus: Hew-Butler et al., Clin J Sport Med 2015

tips.text: Pale straw is the colour you want. Perfectly clear means you can ease off the water a bit.
Eat something plain one to three hours before. Running on a full stomach is a lesson people only need once.
Beyond about an hour to ninety minutes, carbs on the go help: roughly 30 to 60 g an hour, which is a gel or a banana or two.
tips.source: Thomas, Erdman & Burke, Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016

tips.text: Coffee before a run makes it feel easier for many people. It also works on the gut. Know where the toilets are.
tips.source: ISSN caffeine position stand, 2021

tips.text: Runner’s gut trouble is common: a third or more of distance runners get it. Less fibre the night before, and a route that passes a toilet.
tips.source: de Oliveira et al., Sports Med 2014

tips.text: After a run, a normal meal with some protein is all the recovery nutrition most people need. No powder required.
Rain empties the park. Cap on, no cotton, and you get the whole place to yourself. Skin is waterproof.
Cold air will not freeze your lungs; it warms up on the way in. It can make airways sting, so a buff over the mouth helps.
In heat, run by effort and slow down. Heart rate climbs at the same pace when it is warm. Go early, while the pavement is still cool.
In the heat, confusion, stumbling or a sudden headache are not tiredness. Stop, get into shade, cool down with water and get help.
tips.source: ACSM heat illness consensus, Roberts et al. 2023

tips.text: On ice: short steps, aim for the snow rather than the shine, and accept that today is a walk with ambition.
Where there is no pavement, run facing the traffic so you see what is coming. Something that blinks helps too.
tips.source: UK Highway Code, rule 2

tips.text: Wind counts. 5 °C with a strong wind can feel close to zero, especially on the way back when you are sweaty.
Sunscreen on the ears and the back of the neck. Marathon runners showed more sun damage on the skin than non-runners in one study.
tips.source: Ambros-Rudolph et al., Arch Dermatol 2006

tips.text: Dark runs are quieter but uneven. Pick a route you know, with lights, and save the trail for the weekend.
A mild ache that eases as you warm up is usually fine. Pain that gets worse, changes how you run, or is above 3 out of 10 means stop and rest a couple of days.
tips.source: Pain-monitoring model: Silbernagel et al., Am J Sports Med 2007

tips.text: Most running injuries come from doing too much too soon, not from shoes or form. Patience is the best injury prevention there is.
tips.source: Nielsen et al., J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2012

tips.text: A single run much longer than your longest of the past month raised injury risk in a study of over 5,000 runners. Grow it by about 10%.
tips.source: Frandsen et al., Br J Sports Med 2025

tips.text: Shin splints mostly mean too much, too soon. Ease off. A sharp pain on one spot of the bone is different: stop and get it checked.
Static stretching before a run does not prevent injuries. Five minutes of very easy jogging warms you up better.
tips.source: Lauersen et al., Br J Sports Med 2014

tips.text: Strength training cut sports injuries to about a third in a large review. Squats, lunges and calf raises at home count.
tips.source: Lauersen et al., Br J Sports Med 2014

tips.text: Side stitch: slow down, breathe out deeply, press on the spot. Nobody fully knows why they happen, which is oddly comforting.
tips.source: Morton & Callister, Sports Med 2015

tips.text: Sore legs a day or two later after something new is normal. It peaks at around one to three days, then goes.
tips.source: Cheung et al., Sports Med 2003

tips.text: Cramp seems to be more about tired muscles than missing salt. Slow down, stretch gently, walk it off.
tips.source: Schwellnus, Br J Sports Med 2009

tips.text: Leave blisters unpopped if you can, and cover them. Friction plus moisture makes them, so dry socks prevent most.
Chest pain, feeling faint, or a heartbeat that feels wrong: stop and get checked. That is never a toughness test.
Sleep is training. Young athletes sleeping under eight hours were injured more often in one study.
tips.source: Milewski et al., J Pediatr Orthop 2014

tips.text: Back after a break? Start shorter and easier than you were. Fitness returns faster than it first arrived.
Nobody is watching you as much as you think. Students made to wear an embarrassing T-shirt guessed half the room noticed. About a quarter did.
tips.source: Spotlight effect: Gilovich et al., J Pers Soc Psychol 2000

tips.text: You do not need to greet every runner. A small nod is a complete sentence.
Moving among trees or by water lifts mood, and in one large analysis the biggest gain came in the first five minutes.
tips.source: Barton & Pretty, Environ Sci Technol 2010

tips.text: The runner’s high is probably more endocannabinoids than endorphins. Your body makes its own calm, at least in mice, and probably in you.
tips.source: Fuss et al., PNAS 2015

tips.text: Near traffic, keep one ear free, or none. The quiet is part of the run anyway.
Quiet hours: early mornings, rainy evenings, Sunday canal paths, and the industrial estate at the weekend. Nobody runs there. That is the point.
Thinking is allowed. So is not thinking. Both are valid things to do for thirty minutes.
A slow run is data, not a verdict. Most runs are just fine, and fine is the goal.
Even 5 to 10 minutes of running a day was linked to a lower risk of early death in a study of 55,000 adults. Short counts.
tips.source: Lee et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2014

tips.text: Running clubs are lovely. Not wanting one is also lovely. Nobody ever needed permission to run alone.
At a gentle pace you take roughly 1,000 steps per kilometre. Your feet are very good at not complaining about this.
Each landing puts about two to three times your body weight through your leg. Bodies are, frankly, impressive.
Humans are one of very few animals built to run long distances in the heat, mostly thanks to sweating. Embarrassing, but effective.
tips.source: Bramble & Lieberman, Nature 2004

tips.text: Pheidippides, who in legend ran the first marathon, died at the finish. History’s original argument for tapering.
The marathon became 42.195 km at the 1908 London Olympics, so the route could start at Windsor Castle and end in front of the royal box.
In the late 1960s some American joggers were stopped by police, who could not think why anyone would run without being chased.
Kathrine Switzer ran Boston in 1967, when women were not officially allowed. An official tried to drag her off the course. She finished.
Fauja Singh took up running at 89 and finished a marathon at 100. So the “too late to start” argument is, respectfully, weak.
